BEFORE THE FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM GOVERNANCE AND STAKEHOLDER REFORMS  
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
Opening Statement of Abraham Silverman 
I appreciate the invitation to speak to the Commission.  My name is Abe Silverman, and I 
am a research scholar at Johns Hopkins University and principal of SilverGreen Energy 
Consulting, where I write on data centers, interconnection, interregional transmission 
planning, supply chain constraints, and PJM issues, including governance.  I recently 
authored a working paper on “ISO-RTO Governance in the 21st Century,” which goes into 
these matters in more detail.         
Introduction: 
The last 12 months have exposed the structural limitations in PJM’s existing governance 
and stakeholder processes, particularly as the speed and size of large load growth 
overwhelmed the ability of PJM and its stakeholders to respond.  The result has been a 
fractured response that has increased consumer costs and reduced reliability, while, 
paradoxically, creating a challenging environment for investors.      
PJM’s inability to successfully navigate the large-load integration process, along with its 
inability to clear the interconnection backlog or conduct auctions on a predictable 
schedule and with consistent market rules, has put the organization at risk of losing the 
confidence of political actors in the PJM region.  The loss of political support leads directly 
to reduced investor confidence, as investors recognize that the market structure they rely 
on to send price signals is at risk of disintegration.  
The result is that suppliers are increasingly demanding long-term contracts with significant 
risk premiums, even as the supply-demand fundamentals have never looked better for 
merchant investment in PJM, even considering higher capital costs for new generation.  The 
erosion in political confidence also opens the door to calls to move back to re-regulation 
and an increased role for monopoly utilities, which would be a disaster for PJM customers 
on par with the cost overruns and inefficiencies of 1980s markets that gave rise to 
restructuring in the first place. 
Recommendations:    
To begin the process of restoring political (and therefore investor) confidence in PJM 
markets, state actors – including public utility commissions, governors’ offices and state 
legislators – need not only to be given a seat at the table, but also to be treated as full 
partners in solving the complex challenges facing PJM today.  Successfully doing so means

2 
 
reforming PJM’s stakeholder process, its governing documents, and its charge to its Board 
of Managers, and working directly with states to “accommodate, achieve, and adapt” state 
policies,1 or as DOE is currently talking about it, “stabilize, optimize, grow.”2           
Specific recommendations include:  
1) Immediately Form, Fund, and Fully Empower a State-led “States Committee”. 
PJM is a significant outlier in the role it provides its state partners.  Bringing PJM state into 
parity with states in other regional markets should be the starting point for any reform 
efforts.  An immediate “no-regrets” approach would be for the PJM Board of Managers to 
invite states to form a “PJM States Committee” to comprehensively represent the interests 
of states.     
The New England States Committee On Electricity (“NESCOE”) group provides an excellent 
model for how to do this, even in a complicated multi-jurisdictional environment where 
states are not always unified in their policy vision.3  The PJM region would benefit 
enormously from its own states developing a document modeled off of NESCOE’s 2020 
“New England States’ Vision for a Clean, Affordable, and Reliable 21st Century Regional 
Electric Grid,”4 which laid out a comprehensive vision for the ISO New England grid.    
In addition to forming the organization, PJM also needs to fund and fully empower it.   
• In terms of funding, NESCOE’s 2026 budget is $2.7 million for six states with ~1/6 of 
the peak load of PJM.  Costs are collected as part of ISO New England’s network 
transmission charges.  NESCOE’s five employees and consulting budget allows the 
states to access data, conduct modeling and interpret the outcomes. 
• Fully empowering the PJM States Committee means giving the new organization co-
filing rights over, at minimum, the resource adequacy portions of the PJM tariff, 
direct involvement in selecting the PJM Board of Managers, and a mandatory 
consultation relationship with the Board and PJM Management on all topics not 
covered by filing rights.   
• Representatives of the new organization must also be given equivalent participatory 
rights, without requiring sector membership or payment of duplicative membership 
 
1 The “Triple-A” formulation was introduced at the Commission’s 2017 technical conference to explore the 
intersection of state energy policies and wholesale electricity markets in the Northeast.  See Statements of 
Peter Fuller and Abraham Silverman, both of NRG Energy, Inc. in FERC Docket No. AD17-11 (2017). 
2 See U.S. Department of Energy’s 2026 Office of Electricity Strategic Plan.  
3 For a brief history of NESCOE, see the Appendix to “Governance of Multi-State Electricity Markets.” 
4 Issued October 2020, available at:  https://nescoe.com/resource-center/vision-stmt-oct2020/.

3 
 
fees, including the ability to bring issue charges, charter new stakeholder working 
groups, participation in the Liaison Committee, etc.   
A key benefit of a States Committee-type structure is that it brings both political and 
regulatory actors to the stakeholder table, which is necessary if we are to restore state 
confidence in PJM.  The appropriate role is for public service commissions to keep 
participating in the day-to-day stakeholder discussions, and to provide Governors the 
opportunity to create a more policy-oriented body to sit alongside the PJM Board of 
Managers to guide PJM’s strategic direction.  
My observation is that PJM significantly underappreciates the different roles of governor’s 
offices, legislative bodies and state public service commissions.  State commissions – 
represented by the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (“OPSI”) – contribute technical and 
ratemaking expertise, while governors supply long-term vision, political accountability and 
authority to resolve cross-cutting policy tradeoffs.  State statutes typically designate public 
service commissions as quasi-judicial actors, making policy development driven by state 
commissions evolutionary, rather than revolutionary.  And as creatures of statute, state 
commissions often need legislative guidance on how to deal with fast-evolving issues, 
such as the AI revolution.  Governors and legislators, however, can act more quickly, and 
are the appropriate entities to chart a holistic state response to key PJM decisions.    
Finally, it is critical to note that a PJM States Committee would be a complement to, and 
not a replacement of, OPSI.  I would expect OPSI to continue to be a vibrant participant in 
PJM policy.  But for PJM to find its way out of the wilderness, it needs to increase buy-in from 
all sides of state government by means of a more comprehensive representation of states 
in the PJM decision-making processes. 
2) Incorporate a Commitment to Affordability, the Public Interest, and Achievement of 
State Policy into PJM’s Foundational Documents.   
Long-time FERC observers have noted that ISOs and RTOs were initially imagined as mini-
FERCs that would independently call balls and strikes, informed by the “just and 
reasonable” requirements of the Federal Power Act.  Today’s PJM, however, tends to view its 
role largely as representing the interests of its members – not the public interest.     
This broken relationship traces back to PJM’s governing documents, which do not include 
an affirmative obligation to consider the public interest, affordability, or support for state 
policies.  As a Delaware limited liability corporation, PJM has explained that its Board of 
Managers owe their fiduciary duty to the organization, rather than to the public interest.  
Thus, the “scoring rubric” that PJM and its members use to judge their success does not

4 
 
include several of the issues of greatest importance to state policymakers.  Again, PJM is 
out of step with the national consensus on the proper role of an ISO Board.5   
There is no better illustration of PJM’s organizational misalignment with states that the 
issue of large load growth.  There is a startling bipartisan, national, consensus among 
governors and other elected officials that PJM must act promptly to prevent cost shifting 
associated with large load interconnection.  Politically-oriented policy makers6 have been 
exceptionally clear about the need for PJM action in addressing what they characterize as a 
data center-driven affordability crisis.  PJM, however, has been reluctant to engage in 
affordability measures, instead focusing on system reliability (including adding billions in 
Regional Transmission Plan spending to serve new large loads) and incremental changes to 
its market design.7 
To fix this lack of alignment between PJM’s internal rubric and state interests, we need to 
change PJM’s corporate governance documents.  I would recommend three concrete 
changes: 
(1) explicitly incorporate affordability and service to the public interest as core 
priorities in PJM’s foundational documents;  
(2) clarify that the Board of Managers owes its fiduciary duty to the public interest, 
rather than PJM or its members; and  
(3) incorporate support for state policy achievement into its governing objectives.   
PJM often deems affordability as primarily the province of state regulators.8  With no formal 
voice, states are dependent on the organizational priorities set by PJM’s voting members 
and the Board of Managers.  This leaves states with the impossible mission to adapt their 
energy laws and policies without clear wholesale market rules.  This process is less 
efficient and less cost-effective for customers a more effective process would incorporate 
state policy upfront.     
It is surprising to me that PJM’s Board of Managers does not see a commitment to 
affordability as part of PJM’s core mission.  PJM stakeholder discussions often embody the 
“cure to high prices is high prices” mentality, while the organization also acknowledges that 
 
5 For example, MISO is set up as a 501(c)(4) organization “operated exclusively to promote social welfare,” 
while CAISO is set up as a “nonprofit public benefit corporation.”  
6 See the Joint Statement of Principles from the PJM Governors and the National Energy Dominance Council 
and the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, March 4, 2026. 
7 See Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue Fast Path – Large Load Additions, January 16, 2026.  
8 See, e.g., Asim Haque, PJM Senior Vice President, “State frameworks are critical to addressing PJM 
affordability,” Utility Dive, Oct. 2, 2025.

5 
 
interconnection delays, delayed auctions, and the speed and size of large load growth have 
combined to make a normal market response impossible.9   
I note that acknowledging affordability as a key PJM metric does not mean sacrificing 
economic principles or bending to ever-shifting political winds in a way that prioritizes 
short-term rate cuts over long-term customer interests.  Integrating state priorities into 
PJM’s decision-making process aligns investor expectations with politically supportable 
cost-reliability tradeoffs, resulting in stronger, more durable, market outcomes.  Utilities 
are voluntary participants in the ISO/RTO markets and continuation of regional markets 
should not be assumed – particularly if PJM continues to ignore the customer affordability 
issues core to durable regional market structures.  Without affordability, continued state 
political and regulatory support for competitive markets evaporates. 
3) Embrace a “Cooperative Federalism” Approach to Solving the Tough Issues Facing 
PJM. 
PJM should be working directly with state leaders to address key policy challenges at the 
intersection of traditional wholesale-retail boundaries, such as resource adequacy and 
data center load growth.  If there was ever a time when federal and state regulators needed 
to sing from the same hymnal, it is today, as data center load growth threatens to shatter 
our existing electricity market structures. 
This is not a new idea.  The 1935 Federal Power Act explicitly recognized the need for 
shared federal-state jurisdiction over the energy sector and this, at times uneasy, 
relationship between federal and state regulation has existed since the first days of the 
electric industry.10    
Section 209 of the Federal Power Act provides a formal process for the Commission, state 
commissions, and affected public utilities (including PJM) to work through tough issues at 
the edge of federal-state jurisdiction.11  But of course, nothing stops PJM from initiating 
similar action, outside of Section 209.   
Imagine if, instead of PJM’s on-again/off-again approach to mandating data center 
flexibility, the PJM Board had worked directly with state regulators to develop a 
 
9 PJM recognizes these challenges in its “Powering Reliability Through Market Design” paper.   
10 Even as far back as 1938, Professor Frank Strong wrote, “[s]o voluminous is the literature on the perplexing 
problem of federalism that of late it has become the fashion to preface further discussions with something in 
the nature of an apology.”  Cooperative Federalism, 23 IOWA L. REV. 459 at p. 459 (May 1938). 
11 Section 209(b) allows the Commission to “confer with any State commission regarding the relationship 
between rate structures, costs, accounts, charges, practices, classifications, and regulations of public 
utilities subject to the jurisdiction of such State commission and of the Commission[.]”

6 
 
comprehensive federal-state framework for addressing large load growth.  Questions 
regarding jurisdictional limits could have been aired and resolved during the process, 
rather than the uncertainty we still face today.  We would have minimized billions in 
increased costs to ratepayers and established a better investment climate with less 
regulatory uncertainty.  However, this would have meant inverting the stakeholder process 
and recognizing that PJM should be working first and foremost with its state partners in 
developing policy to address this nascent large energy user industry.    
This is a much-needed, high-stakes, conversation.  We need to go beyond critiques of the 
status quo and be willing to do the hard work of reforming PJM’s governance and 
stakeholder process to set PJM up for success into the future.  I appreciate the opportunity 
to be part of that discussion here today.
